content: Monitoring the proportion of leprosy cases among children is preferable because using a small denominator can result in trends that are difficult to interpret. The presence of leprosy in children indicates recent transmission, while its absence may suggest an interruption of transmission, provided there are no inefficiencies in case detection, such as delays in diagnosis. The new child case detection rate is defined as the number of new leprosy cases in children under 15 years of age detected within a specific area and time period (typically one year), expressed per million children in the mid-year population. This indicator serves as a proxy for the incidence of leprosy among children and is more stable than percentages, especially when the number of new cases is small. It also allows for comparisons between different populations. The number of new autochthonous child cases detected refers to the absolute number of new leprosy cases in children under 15 years of age within a specific population and time period. The presence of leprosy in children reflects recent transmission, and this number is useful for forecasting the need for multidrug therapy (MDT) blister packs for children. This indicator is more suitable than the child proportion among new cases, particularly when the total number of new cases is very small (less than 50). The age at the time of detection of leprosy refers to the age of a new autochthonous leprosy case at the time of diagnosis. Age group distributions of new cases detected during a specific period can be represented in a histogram. When comparing different time periods, an increase in the mean age at detection, a shift in the mode toward older age groups, and a decreasing proportion of children among new cases suggest progress toward the elimination of transmission in a country or area. The proportion of cases with MB leprosy among new cases is expressed as a percentage and reflects the proportion of new cases with multibacillary (MB) leprosy among all new cases detected during a specific period. MB leprosy is associated with longer incubation periods, while recent infections are more likely to result in paucibacillary (PB) disease. An increase in the MB proportion among new cases may indicate a decline in transmission or that transmission has already been interrupted. However, variations in definitions over time and incorrect classification (often favoring MB disease) can complicate trend analyses. This cut-off is used because it indicates a higher likelihood that the family member was a source of infection. Cases where the family member was treated before the child was born are not considered. This rate reflects the burden of leprosy relative to the population in the area or country. For autochthonous cases, the numerator is derived by subtracting foreign-born cases from the total number of new cases detected. The number of new autochthonous cases detected refers to the absolute number of new locally acquired cases in a specific population and time period. The goal of leprosy elimination in a given area is zero new autochthonous cases. This indicator is particularly useful when the number of new cases becomes very small. The proportion of foreign-born cases among total new cases detected is expressed as a percentage and reflects the proportion of new cases born abroad among all new cases detected. This indicator reflects the effectiveness of early detection and community awareness. A sporadic autochthonous leprosy case refers to a locally acquired case occurring in an area after the elimination of leprosy has been achieved. If two such cases occur in one year or if cases are reported in two consecutive years, the area’s status is reversed to pre-elimination unless the cases are proven to be unrelated. The pathway to leprosy elimination involves four phases: (1) elimination as a public health problem, (2) interruption of transmission, (3) elimination of leprosy disease, and (4) post-elimination surveillance. A matrix has been developed to guide countries through these phases, with criteria, milestones, and indicators to assess progress. This matrix is also useful for preparing dossiers for verification of elimination by the World Health Organization (WHO). These criteria are assessed through internal and external evaluations, with a focus on achieving zero autochthonous cases and sustaining surveillance for at least ten years post-elimination.
